claim: Male C57Bl/6 mice produce ultrasonic vocalisations in response to the presentation of urine samples from conspecific females in oestrus.
source: Following a previously published protocol (Chabout et al., 2017), we obtained audio recordings of ultrasonic vocalisations emitted by males in response to the presentation of mixtures of urine samples collected from conspecific females in oestrus.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental protocol used to collect male vocalizations, referencing a published method.

claim: Male mouse courtship vocalisations consist of sequences of individual frequency-modulated calls.
source: The vocal patterns emitted in this context consisted of sequences of individual frequency-modulated calls (e.g. see Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1; Holy and Guo, 2005; Chabout et al., 2015; Tschida et al., 2019; Hage et al., 2013; Castellucci et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by both the authors' own data (Figure 1A) and multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The duration of continuous call elements (syllables) in male mouse vocalisations follows a bimodal distribution with a majority of short syllables (local maximum = 23 ms, 86% with durations shorter than 63 ms) and a minority of long syllables (local maximum = 88 ms, 14% with durations longer than 63 ms).
source: Across the set of recorded male vocalisations, the duration of continuous call elements, or syllables, followed a bimodal distribution, with a majority of short syllables (local maximum = 23 ms, 86% [2039/2373] of recorded syllables with durations shorter than 63 ms [local minimum]) and a minority of long syllables (local maximum = 88 ms, 14% [334/2373] of recorded syllables with durations longer than 63 ms, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the authors' recordings shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Male mouse calls are restricted to the ultrasonic frequency range, with maximal energy occurring around 76 kHz and spanning a bandwidth of 16 kHz (68–84 kHz).
source: These male calls were restricted to the ultrasonic frequency range, with the maximal energy in individual syllables occurring around 76 kHz (median peak frequency and 95% confidence interval [CI], 76 ± 0.3 kHz, n = 2373 syllables) and spanning a bandwidth of 16 kHz ([68–84 kHz]; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the authors' data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Individual syllables in male mouse songs are organised in temporally regular sequences with inter-syllable intervals concentrated around 104 ± 2 ms.
source: Individual syllables were organised in temporally regular sequences and often started at an approximately constant time delay from each other (Holy and Guo, 2005; Castellucci et al., 2018), as evidenced by the narrow concentration of inter-syllable interval durations around 104 ± 2 ms (median inter-syllable interval and 95% CI; interquartile range of syllable interval = 61 ms, n = 2322 syllables followed by another syllable within 2 s; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' quantitative data (Figure 1D) and citations to previous studies.

claim: Male courtship songs are attractive to sexually receptive female mice.
source: These courtship songs are attractive to sexually receptive females (Pomerantz et al., 1983), who respond to song playback with approach behaviour (Asaba et al., 2014b; Shepard and Liu, 2011; Chabout et al., 2015; Musolf et al., 2015; Hammerschmidt et al., 2009; Asaba et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating female attraction to male songs.

claim: Male songs facilitate copulatory success.
source: Male songs facilitate copulatory success (Nomoto et al., 2018) and are thought to serve as fitness displays (Egnor and Seagraves, 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mouse listeners are able to detect and report spectro-temporal differences between individual ultrasonic call elements.
source: On the one hand, reinforcement learning experiments have shown that mouse listeners are able to detect and report spectro-temporal differences between individual ultrasonic call elements (Neilans et al., 2014; Holfoth et al., 2014), indicating that mice are perceptually sensitive to a wide range of acoustic features in the vocalisations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reinforcement learning studies.

claim: Female mice use certain acoustic characteristics in male songs to discriminate between social contexts, singer species, strain, and kin.
source: On the other hand, experiments using ethologically relevant place preference paradigms without external reward have shown that females use, or are behaviourally sensitive to, certain acoustic characteristics in male songs to guide social decisions, such as discriminating between social contexts (Chabout et al., 2015), singer species (Musolf et al., 2015), strain (Asaba et al., 2014a; Sugimoto et al., 2011), and kin (Musolf et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Female mice significantly discriminate between song playback and silence in a place preference assay (n = 29 sessions, mean preference index significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, t(28) = 2.81, p=0.0088).
source: The behaviour of female listeners tested in this paradigm significantly discriminated between song playback and silence (n = 29 sessions, mean preference index significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, t(28) = 2.81, p=0.0088; Figure 2H), and mouse listeners were overwhelmingly attracted to the playback of our subset of male songs.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the authors' behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Mouse listeners demonstrate significant approach response after as little as 16.9 s of song playback across four sound presentation trials.
source: Mouse listeners demonstrated significant approach response after as little as 16.9 s of sound playback across the four sound presentation trials (normalised cumulative time in speaker zone significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, p<0.05; Figure 2K), with preference further increasing over the course of song playback.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of temporal data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The sequential organisation of syllables in male songs is not necessary for normal female approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs randomised songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.126, p=0.90).
source: We found that the sequential organisation of syllables in the male songs was not necessary for normal approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs randomised songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.126, p=0.90; Figure 3A, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and randomized songs.

claim: Temporal reversal of vocal sequences does not significantly affect female approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs reversed songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = –1.46, p=0.16).
source: Temporal reversal of the vocal sequence did not significantly affect females' approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs reversed songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = –1.46, p=0.16; Figure 3C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and reversed songs.

claim: Female listeners are not relying on global cues reflecting the overall structure of male song sequences when selecting which sound source to approach.
source: Together, these observations suggest that female listeners are not relying on global cues reflecting the overall structure of male song sequences when selecting which sound source to approach.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the results of multiple manipulations (randomization and reversal) showing no behavioral effect.

claim: Females approach intact and phase-scrambled song playback similarly (mean preference index in response to intact vs phase-scrambled songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(22) = –0.27, p=0.79).
source: Females approached the intact and phase-scrambled song playback similarly (mean preference index in response to intact vs phase-scrambled songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(22) = –0.27, p=0.79; Figure 3E, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and phase-scrambled songs.

claim: Comparing intact songs with sequences of pure tones at the peak syllable frequency (76 kHz) fails to elicit differential approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs pure tone sequences did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.034, p=0.97).
source: Second, comparing intact songs with more drastically simplified sound sequences that stripped down each syllable into a pure tone at the peak syllable frequency (76 kHz) also failed to elicit differential approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs pure tone sequences did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.034, p=0.97; Figure 3G and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact songs and pure tone sequences.

claim: Female behaviour is robust to the removal of fast spectro-temporal structure in syllables when sound energy is still present at the natural syllable peak frequency.
source: Together, these findings show that female behaviour was robust to the removal of fast spectro-temporal structure in the syllables, at least when sound energy was still present at the natural syllable peak frequency.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the results of phase-scrambling and pure tone manipulations showing no behavioral effect.

claim: Females are highly sensitive to the disruption of song temporal regularity and preferentially approach intact over irregular song playback (mean preference index in response to intact vs irregular songs significantly differed from zero, one-sample t-test, t(23) = 3.43, p=0.00023).
source: Interestingly, females were highly sensitive to the disruption of song temporal regularity and preferentially approached intact over irregular song playback (mean preference index in response to intact vs irregular songs significantly differed from zero, one-sample t-test, t(23) = 3.43, p=0.00023, Figure 4E, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and temporally irregular songs.

claim: Mouse listeners start to show sustained preference for regular over irregular songs after 85.4 s of sound playback.
source: On average, mouse listeners started to show this sustained preference for regular over irregular songs after 85.4 s of sound playback (normalised cumulative time in speaker zone significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, p<0.05; Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Female listeners do not show consistent behavioural preference when playback of intact songs is contrasted with super-regular songs (one-sample t-test, t(21) = 1.48, p=0.15).
source: Female listeners did not show any consistent behavioural preference when the playback of intact songs was contrasted with that of super-regular songs (one-sample t-test, t(21) = 1.48, p=0.15; Figure 4H, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and super-regular songs.

claim: The rhythmicity of natural male songs is already sufficiently salient to reach the criterion for approach behaviour by female listeners and cannot be improved by additional regularisation of syllable onsets.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rhythmicity of natural male songs is already sufficiently salient to reach the criterion for approach behaviour by female listeners and cannot be improved by additional regularisation of syllable onsets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of preference for super-regular over intact songs.

claim: Female mice monitor temporal regularity in male songs during courtship behaviour.
source: The results show that female mice monitor temporal regularity in male songs, while their behaviour was unaffected by changes in the song sequential organisation or the fine acoustic structure of individual syllables.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from multiple behavioral experiments.

claim: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic signature of singer fitness.
source: The findings highlight the selective extraction of song temporal regularity, which may be an acoustic signature of singer fitness, as an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during goal-directed social behaviour.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Neurons across the mouse auditory system are tuned to different spectro-temporal features in song syllables.
source: On the one hand, neurons across the mouse auditory system are tuned to different spectro-temporal features in song syllables, and mouse listeners have been shown to be perceptually sensitive to, or able to detect, the acoustic manipulations of individual syllables used in the current study.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about auditory system tuning properties.

claim: Externally rewarded reinforcement learning and associated sharpening of sensory acuity and neuronal tuning likely bias and amplify the perceptual ability of a naive animal.
source: However, such externally rewarded reinforcement learning and the associated sharpening of sensory acuity and neuronal tuning likely bias and amplify the perceptual ability of a naive animal (Fritz et al., 2005; Fritz et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on perceptual learning.

claim: In naturalistic settings, social behaviour requires the selective monitoring of specific informative sensory features while cognitively suppressing or ignoring other dimensions that may be perceptible.
source: On the other hand, social behaviour in naturalistic settings requires the selective monitoring of specific informative sensory features, while cognitively suppressing or ignoring other dimensions that may however be perceptible, as classically demonstrated in the toad's visual system during prey capture (Wachowitz and Ewert, 1996).
evidence: The claim draws on established principles from sensory neuroscience, supported by a citation to work in toads.

claim: In the context of ethologically valid behaviour, female listeners show behavioural invariance to several acoustic features that they are, or can be trained to become, perceptually sensitive to.
source: Our work complements previous studies that quantified the upper bounds of mouse hearing sensitivity. We show that, in the context of an ethologically valid behaviour, female listeners show behavioural invariance to several acoustic features that they are, or can be trained to become, perceptually sensitive to.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Songs from male mice demonstrate characteristic sequential features, with short syllables typically dominating the beginning of a vocal phrase.
source: Indeed, songs from male mice have been shown to demonstrate some characteristic sequential features, with short syllables typically dominating the beginning of a vocal phrase (Chabout et al., 2015; Matsumoto and Okanoya, 2016; Castellucci et al., 2018; Castellucci et al., 2016; Hertz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies characterizing song structure.

claim: During courtship behaviour, females monitor the presence/absence or relative occurrence of specific syllable types independent of the syllable order.
source: While mouse listeners are known to perceptually discriminate between syllable types differing in their spectro-temporal features (Neilans et al., 2014), our finding that female approach behaviour was not affected by a shuffling of the syllable sequence indicates that, during courtship behaviour, females monitor the presence/absence or relative occurrence of specific syllable types, or other acoustic features of the songs, independent of the syllable order.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral invariance to syllable order randomization.

claim: Chabout et al., 2015 showed that female listeners discriminated between syntactically simple and complex songs produced by males in different social contexts.
source: Our result also disambiguates previous findings on mouse sensitivity to syntactic information in male songs: Chabout et al., 2015 previously showed, in a similar behavioural paradigm, that female listeners discriminated between syntactically simple and complex songs produced by males in different social contexts.
evidence: The claim describes findings from a previous study.

claim: Listeners may have been primarily exploiting differences in repertoire composition rather than syllable sequencing to discriminate songs produced from different social contexts.
source: Songs produced in the two tested social contexts differed both in the first-order syllable sequencing and in the composition of the syllable repertoire. Our finding on females' behavioural insensitivity to syllable order thus suggests that listeners may have been primarily exploiting differences in repertoire composition to discriminate and ultimately select songs produced from a specific social context.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the current study's findings about syllable order insensitivity, reinterpreting previous results.

claim: Female listeners do not strongly rely on the global structure of the syllable sequence during courtship behaviour.
source: Thus, our results show that female listeners do not strongly rely on the global structure of the syllable sequence during courtship behaviour.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from manipulations of global song structure.

claim: Sound energy in and around a critical band corresponding to the syllable frequency range, displayed at the natural temporal organisation of male songs, is a sufficient approximation of male courtship songs to drive female approach behaviour.
source: Thus, the evidence suggests that sound energy in and around a critical band corresponding to the syllable frequency range, displayed at the natural temporal organisation of male songs, is a sufficient approximation of male courtship songs to drive female approach behaviour.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral results with pure tone sequences and the discussion of previous studies.

claim: As long as the temporal structure of pup calls is maintained, pup retrieval behaviour is robust to the removal of most of the spectral structure of ultrasonic pup isolation calls.
source: Our and others' results on female courtship behaviour complement the body of work on maternal behaviour by lactating mothers: as long as the temporal structure of pup calls is maintained, pup retrieval behaviour is robust to the removal of most of the spectral structure of ultrasonic pup isolation calls (Ehret and Haack, 1982), and three-harmonic stack approximations of sonic wriggling calls elicit normal maternal responses (Gaub and Ehret, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on maternal behavior.

claim: The intelligibility of speech degraded in the spectral domain remains partially preserved if it is shaped with the correct amplitude envelopes.
source: Similar importance of temporal patterns for the perception of social communication, over the fine acoustic structure of individual elements, has been demonstrated behaviourally in other animal species, including humans: as illustrated in vocoded speech, the intelligibility of speech degraded in the spectral domain remains partially preserved if it is shaped with the correct amplitude envelopes (Shannon et al., 1995; Van Tasell et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on human speech perception.

claim: Temporal regularity in the song is the only feature observed to be extracted by female listeners from male acoustic courtship displays among the subset of acoustic features tested in this study.
source: Of the subset of acoustic features tested in this study, temporal regularity in the song was the only feature we observed to be extracted by female listeners from male acoustic courtship displays.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding from the series of behavioral experiments.

claim: Temporal regularity is attractive to females in the context of vocal-based mate selection.
source: We found that mouse listeners preferentially approached intact over irregular courtship songs, suggesting that regularity is attractive to females in the context of vocal-based mate selection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral preference for regular over irregular songs.

claim: The temporal regularity observed in mouse songs is a consequence of breathing patterns regulating the production of syllables by the emitter as individual calls are generated following the onset of exhalation.
source: The temporal regularity observed in mouse songs is a consequence of breathing patterns regulating the production of syllables by the emitter as individual calls are generated following the onset of exhalation (Tschida et al., 2019; Castellucci et al., 2018; Sirotin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on vocal production mechanisms.

claim: Disruption to the temporal regularity of male song may result from irregular breathing cycles and thus 'stuttering' singing by the male, or by the inability to sustain bouts of vocal production of sufficient duration.
source: Disruption to the temporal regularity of male song, as artificially introduced in this study, may, for instance, result from irregular breathing cycles and thus 'stuttering' singing by the male, or by the inability to sustain bouts of vocal production of sufficient duration to elicit a salient percept of regularity in the listener.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential biological mechanisms underlying temporal irregularity.

claim: Songs by Foxp2 knockout mice contain rhythmic irregularities.
source: A recent study of courtship songs by Foxp2 knockout mice provided direct evidence for a link between male emitter fitness and song temporal regularity by showing songs by mutant mice contain rhythmic irregularities (Castellucci et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on Foxp2 knockout mice.

claim: Temporal predictability facilitates auditory detection of near-threshold stimuli compared to an identical aperiodic sequence.
source: From the perspective of the listener, temporal predictability has been shown to facilitate auditory detection of near-threshold stimuli compared to an identical aperiodic sequence (Lawrance et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on temporal predictability.

claim: In human listeners, speech intelligibility is disrupted by temporal jittering of sentences.
source: Additionally, in human listeners, speech intelligibility is disrupted by temporal jittering the sentences (Ghitza and Greenberg, 2009; Pichora-Fuller et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on human speech perception.

claim: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic cue signalling the fitness or suitability of the potential mating partner to the listener.
source: Thus, perhaps by improving the perceptual signal-to-noise ratio of male courtship songs, temporal regularity may represent an acoustic cue signalling the fitness or suitability of the potential mating partner to the listener (Egnor and Seagraves, 2016), to which we show that socially motivated listeners are highly attuned to.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Natural mouse songs might already be at ceiling in terms of the perceptual saliency of their temporal regularity and their attractiveness to female listeners.
source: Female behaviour did not appear to discriminate between intact songs and an artificial 'super-regular' version of the songs, suggesting that natural mouse songs might already be at ceiling in terms of the perceptual saliency of their temporal regularity, and therefore, their attractiveness to female listeners.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of preference for super-regular songs.

claim: Neuronal responses in barrel cortex respond indistinguishably to lightly temporally jittered and perfectly regular sequences of whisker deflections when the stimulus presentation rate is slower than 20 Hz.
source: In the somatosensory system, neuronal responses in barrel cortex responded indistinguishably to lightly temporally jittered and perfectly regular sequences of whisker deflections, when the stimulus presentation rate was slower than 20 Hz (Lak et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on somatosensory processing.

claim: At natural syllable rates of mouse songs, removing low temporal jitter present in intact songs to create super-regular songs may not significantly impact perceptually relevant neuronal substrates.
source: In a hypothesis that remains to be directly tested in the auditory system, it is thus possible that, at the natural syllable rates of mouse songs, removing the low temporal jitter present in intact songs to create super-regular songs does not significantly impact on perceptually relevant neuronal substrates.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis based on findings from the somatosensory system.

claim: The syllable rate in mouse songs (~7 Hz) broadly matches with that of other mammalian vocal patterns such as monkey vocalisations and human speech.
source: The syllable rate in mouse songs (~7 Hz; Holy and Guo, 2005) broadly matches with that of other mammalian vocal patterns such as monkey vocalisations and human speech (Ghazanfar and Takahashi, 2014; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on vocal patterns across species.

claim: The stimulus presentation rate in mouse songs is directly determined by the breathing rhythm of the singer.
source: On the one hand, this stimulus presentation rate in mouse songs is directly determined by the breathing rhythm of the singer.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about vocal production mechanisms.

claim: Active sensation during whisking and sniffing operates within the frequency range of both respiratory-coupled oscillations and the hippocampal theta rhythm in rodents.
source: Given that active sensation during whisking and sniffing operates within the frequency range of both respiratory-coupled oscillations (Tort et al., 2018) and the hippocampal theta rhythm in rodents (Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Kepecs et al., 2007; Grion et al., 2016; Kleinfeld et al., 2016), similar constraints may be placed on the cortical mechanisms of hearing (Schroeder et al., 2010), especially during natural behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on sensory processing and oscillations.

claim: The syllable rate in mouse songs generally corresponds to the timescale of slow amplitude envelope in human speech, which contributes to the identification of both prosodic and syllabic content.
source: On the other hand, the syllable rate in mouse songs generally corresponds to the timescale of slow amplitude envelope in human speech, which is known to contribute to the identification of both prosodic and syllabic content (Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on speech processing.

claim: Vocal sequences such as human speech and mouse songs contain sufficiently salient temporal regularity to allow listeners to make predictions about the incoming signal.
source: While vocal sequences such as human speech and mouse songs are quasi-periodic rather than metronomically regular signals, they both contain sufficiently salient temporal regularity to allow listeners to make predictions about the incoming signal (Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on speech processing.

claim: Cortical theta oscillations in the 4–8 Hz range entrain to the slow temporal envelope modulations in speech and may play a role in parsing continuous sensory input by coordinating neuronal excitability to optimally support the decoding of phonemes.
source: An influential model of speech processing proposes that cortical theta oscillations in the 4–8 Hz range entrain to the slow temporal envelope modulations in speech and may play a role in parsing continuous sensory input by coordinating neuronal excitability to optimally support the decoding of phonemes (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous theoretical model of speech processing.

claim: The results identify a key role of temporal regularity, but invariance to global and local song structure, in the goal-directed use of vocal patterns by female listeners.
source: In summary, we used an ethologically driven approach to evaluate the behavioural relevance of several acoustic features in mouse communication. Our results identify a key role of temporal regularity, but invariance to global and local song structure, in the goal-directed use of vocal patterns by female listeners.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The selective monitoring of temporal regularity in communication sounds is an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during mammalian vocal perception.
source: The findings highlight the selective monitoring of temporal regularity in communication sounds as an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during mammalian vocal perception.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the findings, proposing evolutionary significance.

claim: A total of 83 female C57Bl/6J inbred mice participated in the experiments.
source: A total of 83 female C57Bl/6J inbred mice (Mus musculus, Charles River Laboratories, UK) participated in the experiments.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Mice participated in the playback experiments between the ages of 5–11 wk (mean = 9 wk).
source: Mice participated in the playback experiments between the ages of 5–11 wk (mean = 9 wk; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the age range of experimental subjects.

claim: The stimulus set used in playback experiments consisted of seven distinct songs produced by C57BL/6 male mice aged 22 wk on average (median age, range [10–27 wk]).
source: This stimulus set was composed of seven distinct songs produced by C57BL/6 male mice aged 22 wk on average (median age, range [10–27 wk]) in response to the presentation of female urine.
evidence: The claim describes the characteristics of the acoustic stimuli used.

claim: The songs varied in duration, lasting on average 33.4 s (median duration, range [13–41 s]), and were composed of an average of 145 syllables (median, range [95–186]).
source: The songs varied in duration, lasting on average 33.4 s (median duration, range [13–41 s]), and were composed of an average of 145 syllables (median, range [95–186]).
evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the song stimuli.

claim: Olfactory stimulation from mixed male bedding samples was present throughout the testing session to increase sexual arousal and motivation in female listeners.
source: Importantly, olfactory stimulation from mixed male bedding samples placed under each of the loudspeakers was present throughout the testing session in order to increase sexual arousal and motivation in the female listeners (Hammerschmidt et al., 2009; Asaba et al., 2014a) and create a multisensory coherent approximation of a natural social situation.
evidence: The claim describes an experimental design feature supported by citations.

claim: Young female C57Bl/6 mice participated once in the playback experiment while in the fertile (proestrus or oestrus) stage of their oestrous cycle.
source: Young female C57Bl/6 mice (aged 5–11 wk; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) participated once in the playback experiment, while in the fertile (proestrus or oestrus) stage of their oestrous cycle (as assessed by vaginal cytology, see 'Methods').
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol for subject selection.

claim: The preference for song over silence was robust to different lengths of the speaker zone used to calculate the preference index.
source: The preference for song over silence was robust to different lengths of the speaker zone used to calculate the preference index (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim describes a control analysis showing robustness of the main finding.

claim: The build-up of preferential approach to song was evident in the vast majority of animals and mostly sustained over a behavioural session.
source: The build-up of preferential approach to song was evident in the vast majority of animals, mostly sustained over a behavioural session (Figure 2L), and similar across the four sound presentation trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim describes the temporal dynamics of the behavioral response shown in figures.

claim: The lack of sensitivity to syllable sequence structure was not caused by the selection of specific temporal or spatial parameters for analysis.
source: This confirms that the lack of sensitivity to syllable sequence structure we observe here was not caused by the selection of specific temporal or spatial parameters for analysis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from control analyses showing robustness across different parameters.

claim: This behavioural invariance to changes in the syllable order was apparent at all timepoints of song set playback as well as at different speaker zone lengths.
source: This behavioural invariance to changes in the syllable order was apparent at all timepoints of song set playback (Figure 3B), as well as at different speaker zone lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), and was comparable across the four sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of the finding.

claim: This lack of behavioural sensitivity to song temporal reversal was present throughout sound playback in the vast majority of animals tested.
source: This lack of behavioural sensitivity to song temporal reversal was present throughout sound playback in the vast majority of animals tested (Figure 3D), across the sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and for different spatial regions of interest (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim describes the consistency of the behavioral finding across different analyses.

claim: These two instances of behavioural insensitivity to changes in the syllable acoustic trajectories were robust to variations in temporal and spatial parameters used for analysis.
source: These two instances of behavioural insensitivity to changes in the syllable acoustic trajectories were robust to variations in temporal (Figure 3F and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) and spatial (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and G) parameters used for analysis.
evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of findings.

claim: The interquartile range of syllable interval in irregular songs is 134 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs.
source: To do this, we generated a set of temporally irregular songs that consisted of the same syllable sequence with a broadened distribution of silent pauses compared to intact songs (interquartile range of syllable interval in irregular songs = 134 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs; Figure 4A, B and E, left, and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the manipulated stimuli.

claim: The sensitivity to temporal regularity was robust and similarly strong across all sizes of speaker zones.
source: The sensitivity to temporal regularity was robust and similarly strong across all sizes of speaker zones (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim describes a control analysis showing robustness of the finding.

claim: The temporal profile of approach behaviour of a majority of animals favoured intact, regular songs over the course of a session and across sound presentation trials.
source: The temporal profile of approach behaviour of a majority of animals favoured intact, regular songs over the course of a session (Figure 4G), and across sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the consistency of the behavioral response shown in figures.

claim: The longer latency to behavioural discrimination after song onset when discriminating between two concurrent sound streams compared to approaching intact song playback over silence might reflect the need for additional accumulation of evidence and temporal integration.
source: This longer latency to behavioural discrimination after song onset compared to when approaching intact song playback over silence (16.9 s, Figure 2K) might reflect the need for additional accumulation of evidence and temporal integration when discriminating between the two concurrent sound streams.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the difference in response latencies.

claim: The interquartile range of syllable interval in super-regular songs is 24 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs.
source: To this end, we created a set of highly rhythmic songs in which the silent breaks were modified such that the onset of the syllables in each song occurred exactly at the dominant inter-syllable interval, effectively narrowing the distribution of inter-syllable times (interquartile range of syllable interval in super-regular songs = 24 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs; Figure 4C, D and H, left, and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the manipulated stimuli.

claim: This behavioural invariance to improvements of the songs' temporal regularity remained when tested at different timepoints during song playback or using different spatial parameters for analysis.
source: This behavioural invariance to improvements of the songs' temporal regularity remained when tested at different timepoints during song playback (Figure 4I) or using different spatial parameters for analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of the finding.

claim: Sessions in which the animal displayed a clear side bias were excluded from the analysis (29% ± 7% of behavioural sessions excluded due to side bias, mean and 95% CI).
source: Sessions in which the animal displayed a clear side bias (consistent preference for the left or right side of the behavioural box despite changes in the sound playback side, evaluated as all four trials showing a positive, or all negative, difference between the times in the left and right speaker zones) were excluded from the analysis (29% ± 7% of behavioural sessions excluded due to side bias, mean and 95% CI).
evidence: The claim describes the data exclusion criteria and the proportion of excluded sessions.
